Online Event Tuesday, 22 September 2026 10am Washington, DC | 4pm Brussels | 5pm Sanaa Please register here if you would like to attend this online event. Over the past week, the Houthis have swept down Yemen’s western coast and reached Bab al-Mandab, unravelling a defensive line that had held for years, and exposing just how fragmented the government camp’s forces had become. A string of retreats was decisive, as the National Resistance, Giants Brigades and other nominally allied units, each with its own command and backers, lost Khokha, Mokha and the roads linking Taiz, Hodeida and the coast, fighting side by side but never as one army. A foothold near one of the world’s busiest shipping chokepoints gives the Houthis fresh leverage over Saudi Arabia, just as Riyadh’s containment strategy is under strain. It also ties their campaign more closely to Iran’s entrenched standoff with Washington: any disruption to shipping through Bab al-Mandab would compound the effects of restrictions around the Strait of Hormuz, raising the economic costs of a wider confrontation. In this online event, Crisis Group brings together leading experts to discuss how the front collapsed so quickly, what the new balance of power means for Taiz, Marib and the other fronts still in play, and whether Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government and Yemen’s neighbours can keep this round of fighting from sliding into a wider war. Panellists: April Longley Alley | Senior Fellow, The Washington Institute Ahmed Nagi | Senior Analyst, Yemen, Crisis Group Peter Salisbury | Adjunct Professor, Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs Moderator: Yasmine Farouk | Project Director, Gulf and Arabian Peninsula, Crisis Group The panel discussion will be held in English and will be live-streamed on YouTube . 0 0

A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria eschelhaas Thu, 09/17/2026 - 12:17 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Syrian President Ahmed Al-Shara, right, and Syrian Democratic Forces commander Mazloum Abdi, left, attend a session at the presidential palace in Damascus. Rami Alsayed / NurPhoto / via AFP Commentary / Middle East & North Africa 17 September 2026 15 minutes A Pivotal Moment in Uniting Post-Assad Syria The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which long enjoyed de facto autonomy in north-eastern Syria, have dissolved. But tensions in the region remain high as talks about integration with the central state proceed. Further compromise would set a useful precedent for other parts of the country. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Syria The scene on 25 August, like countless others in Syria of late, would have been unimaginable a mere two years ago. Mazloum Abdi, commander-in-chief of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), the Kurdish-led group that had autonomously run much of the country’s north east for some fourteen years, stood in Damascus beside the flag of Syria’s former opposition and new state, announcing the SDF’s dissolution and taking on the role of adviser to President Ahmad al-Sharaa. Beyond marking Abdi’s transition to senior government official, the event represented a pivotal moment in the process aimed at integrating the SDF’s institutions into the Syrian state. Damascus and the SDF leadership have come a long way since their troops clashed in early 2026, but difficult questions lie ahead as they continue talks to define the next phase of integration. Deepening cooperation – and providing further clarity to address Syrian Kurds’ concerns about their security and role in governance – is the best way forward. Progress amid Frustration While it has made important progress, the SDF integration process has also been bumpy, generating its fair share of frustrations. Disappointment is particularly acute among the group’s core Kurdish constituency: the deal reached in late August is the latest in a series of compromises leaving the north east far less autonomy than it had enjoyed during most of Syria’s civil war. The shortfall is due partly to the dramatic shift in U.S. policy following the fall of former President Bashar al-Assad’s Baathist regime, as Washington embraced al-Sharaa’s government and wound down its decade-long partnership with the SDF. But the SDF’s own miscalculations also played a role. After agreeing with Damascus in March 2025 to define integration arrangements by year’s end, it dragged its feet. That strategy proved ill-advised. Government forces pressed their advantage on the battlefield in January, and the SDF saw its hand weaken. Tensions prompted by this confrontation linger to this day. Still, the integration process has proven successful in several key respects. It ended weeks of armed conflict that, just nine months ago, threatened to plunge northern Syria into further violence along ethnic lines; secured unprecedented Syrian government commitments to Kurdish rights; enabled the return of thousands of Kurdish families to their homes after years of displacement, partially reversing war-induced demographic changes; and improved prospects for separate talks in neighbouring Türkiye that aim to end decades of insurgency by the Kurdistan Workers Party or PKK, with which the SDF has deep ties. Scepticism of integration runs deep among Kurds, even as prominent Arab voices call for accelerating it. The SDF’s official dissolution marks the beginning of a new, critical phase. Important gaps between the sides remain, notably over the degree to which former SDF-aligned institutions can maintain coherence as they become part of state structures. The parties will also have to contend with countervailing popular pressures in the north east – scepticism of integration runs deep among Kurds, even as prominent Arab voices call for accelerating it. Unrest following the killing of a Kurdish soldier on 10 September has deepened the polarisation. If Damascus and the former SDF leadership can address these issues together, they could simultaneously consolidate the state’s writ and provide the former SDF with substantive roles in local and central governance. This outcome would do more than benefit both sides; it also could help clarify options for addressing similar challenges in other parts of a country still recovering from years of brutal civil war. A Series of Negotiations The ceremony on 25 August marked the latest in a series of understandings between the SDF and the central state. The first one, reached in March 2025, was very broadly framed and left many issues unresolved; months of deadlock in talks aimed at fleshing it out gave way to weeks of armed confrontation in early 2026. The subsequent 29 January agreement broke the impasse, reflecting the decisive shift in the balance of power after the government’s rapid military advance. This deal outlined a partial framework for integrating the troops, institutions and lands under SDF control into the Syrian state, but it did not answer key questions concerning the degree and pace of assimilation, among other practical details. Talks continued between the two sides to iron out these issues. At one level, they involved President al-Sharaa, Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani, Mazloum Abdi and other senior north-eastern figures, who met occasionally to overcome key obstacles. Day-to-day discussions were left to a team appointed by al-Sharaa, working alongside former senior SDF officials named to government positions and other influential figures in the north east. U.S. diplomats, led by presidential envoy Tom Barrack, supported the process, but with a much lighter touch than during the direct mediation in which they engaged throughout much of 2025. Inevitably, these talks reflected the new balance of power that tilted heavily in the central state’s favour after the SDF’s military setback. The organisation nonetheless retained leverage, however diminished: as SDF leaders were well aware, Damascus was eager for them to officially dissolve the group and thus demonstrate their genuine commitment to integration. Weeks of intermittent exchanges centred on two issues in particular: the roles senior north-eastern figures would play in the central government and the scope of Kurdish-language instruction in schools. Kurdish representation at such senior levels of state power is a clear departure from the decades of exclusion and neglect the community endured under Baathist rule. The two sides finally reached a package of understandings on those matters in the hours preceding the SDF’s 25 August dissolution announcement. Mazloum Abdi agreed to become a presidential adviser, while Ilham Ahmad, head of the SDF’s external relations and a central player in the negotiations, assented to taking a seat in the Syrian parliament. These positions are of a lower rank than those informally suggested by SDF leaders, U.S. officials and other intermediaries, who had floated the idea of Abdi serving on Syria’s new national security council and Ahmad assuming a senior foreign ministry post. Nevertheless, they offer Kurdish leaders a foothold in the central government, supplementing key roles already filled by (former) SDF figures in the nascent integrated military and security structures in the north east. These include Sipan Hemo (until January, a leading SDF figure, now serving as assistant minister of defence for the north east) and Mahmoud Khalil Ali (aka “Siamand Afrin”), who previously led the SDF’s Asayesh security forces and is now deputy head of state security forces in the Hassaka governorate. Kurdish representation at such senior levels of state power is a clear departure from the decades of exclusion and neglect the community endured under Baathist rule. The two sides likewise reached a compromise on Kurdish-language education. Under the SDF-aligned administration, Kurdish had been the prevalent language of instruction in most classes offered in Kurdish areas. As the central government assumes responsibility for schools throughout the north east, SDF negotiators had aimed to maintain as much Kurdish-language instruction as possible. At first, Damascus wanted to limit Kurdish-language classes to just two hours per week. In the end, the central government agreed that schools in areas where Kurds form a significant percentage of the population would provide three hours weekly of Kurdish-language instruction and a fourth hour of “activities” in Kurdish. It also consented to having four core subjects – social studies, history, geography and philosophy – offered in Kurdish during the current academic year, albeit not necessarily beyond that. This compromise built on Damascus’s decision in June to recognise diplomas previously issued by the SDF-linked administration. It also expanded on points outlined in a decree issued by al-Sharaa in January – which, in addition to broader commitments on Kurdish rights, acknowledged Kurdish as a national language and permitted elective Kurdish-language courses. Though the August agreement went beyond Damascus’s previous positions, it still fell short of aspirations held by many Syrian Kurds. In subsequent days, Kurdish organisations (including some allied with the SDF) demonstrated in favour of expanded Kurdish instruction. In a nod to those demands, Mazloum Abdi noted in his remarks announcing the SDF’s dissolution that “we will work to implement this decision [on education] in the current year, so that we can build on it in the future”. Gaps Ahead Meanwhile, other files remain subject to further negotiation. The two sides have yet to fully agree on how members of the SDF’s Women’s Protection Units (in Kurdish, Yekîneyên Parastina Jinê , or YPJ) will be incorporated into government forces. Damascus rebuffed SDF proposals to integrate the all-women force into Syria’s nascent post-Assad military, which currently excludes women from combat units. It suggested instead that they be placed under the interior ministry, which in recent months has begun recruiting women throughout the country into police forces. SDF and YPJ leaders have signalled openness to this idea in principle, while pushing to maintain the YPJ’s structural coherence and focus on counter-terrorism , building on its role in combating ISIS. Damascus and Kurdish leaders continued discussing this matter amid their late August meetings, but they have yet to reach an understanding. Beyond these immediate practical gaps lies a more essential divergence that has marked negotiations since early 2025, namely over how centralised each side believes the new Syrian state should be, and thus over how to define integration , particularly in Kurdish population centres. Both concur that the north east should be fully incorporated within state institutions, but they differ on the degree to which former SDF-linked structures, military as well as civilian, should be able to retain their coherence and the extent to which authority would be locally delegated. To date, Damascus has been prepared to live with a light-touch integration of Kurdish entities into the all-important military and security sectors. To date, Damascus has been prepared to live with a light-touch integration of Kurdish entities into the all-important military and security sectors, with SDF and Asayesh forces maintaining much of their structural integrity under the command of senior officers appointed by Damascus. As a result, Kurdish residents’ primary day-to-day interaction with government forces in the north east has been with Kurdish personnel reporting to an integrated chain of command. Such was still the case after the central state sent more of its forces to the region, most recently through the 1 September deployment of additional personnel to Hassaka city. The approach appears to have been largely successful, extending the reach of state sovereignty throughout the north east while keeping public safety in local hands and mitigating concerns among Kurds about how they would fare with non-Kurdish forces. But the written agreements the sides have signed thus far do not clearly define the terms of these arrangements. Nor do they indicate how long the arrangements will stay in place, leaving open the question of whether and to what extent Damascus might push to deepen central authority as time goes by. This ambiguity was a key reason why the SDF repeatedly advocated for solidifying the understandings through some form of constitutional guarantee. Damascus demurred, deferring talks about that demand to forthcoming discussions of Syria’s future constitution. Kurdish leaders have also made clear their intention to press in those discussions for more explicit constitutional linguistic and cultural protections. The timeframe and process for drafting the constitution remain uncertain, as does the mechanism that would allow for input by Kurdish leaders. Addressing Challenges, Clarifying Gains Beyond these gaps, three challenges stand out: returning displaced persons to their homes; managing incidents that threaten to ignite ethnic and political tensions; and addressing the sharp cost-of-living increase that is, at least in part, a by-product of integration. The issue of displaced persons counts among the most sensitive in northern Syria. Both Kurds and Arabs suffered large-scale displacement during the civil war, with tens of thousands of Kurds forced to leave their homes during offensives in which Syrian opposition forces backed by Türkiye seized the district of Afrin (in north-western Syria) and the towns of Ras al-Ayn and Tel Abyadh (in the north east) from Kurdish-led forces allied with the SDF. Thousands of Arab residents also fled during various SDF advances. Some of the resulting demographic changes persist to this day, exacerbating ethnic tensions that for decades were stoked by the forced Arabisation policies of Bashar al-Assad and his father, Hafez. Both Damascus and Kurdish leaders assert that securing the safe return of displaced persons is a priority. Both Damascus and Kurdish leaders assert that securing the safe return of displaced persons is a priority, and they have restated their commitment to that goal at every stage of negotiations. Together, they have achieved significant progress since the 29 January agreement. Between March and July, some 11,000 families returned to Afrin in convoys organised by government officials (including Damascus appointees and former SDF figures) in coordination with a committee representing the displaced. The influx of returnees has helped both restore Afrin’s social fabric and mitigate concerns among senior Kurdish figures who harboured doubts about integration. The government launched a similar cooperative effort to facilitate returns to and around Ras al-Ayn, an ethnically mixed town known in Kurdish as Serê Kaniyê. Yet serious obstacles have emerged of late. On 10 August, armed men attacked the first convoy carrying Kurdish families returning to Ras al-Ayn. As reports of violence spread, demonstrations erupted in Kurdish population centres in the north east, with a number of protesters reportedly attempting to break into central government facilities. Competing narratives of what motivated the attacks are difficult to parse, and no settled account has emerged. Kurdish leaders and government officials worked together to restore calm, with Mazloum Abdi calling for demonstrators to preserve state institutions and government forces announcing the arrest of several Ras al-Ayn assailants. The incident nevertheless underscored the limits of state authority in an area that until 2025 was controlled by poorly disciplined rebel factions, which seized it from the SDF during a Turkish-backed offensive in 2019. Those factions have since been incorporated into state forces, but their assimilation is far from complete. The government suspended returns to Ras al-Ayn town until conditions improve, which will entail addressing property disputes and dampening ethnic tensions in a location awash with guns. Their success in developing a cooperative model notwithstanding, the government and Kurdish leaders face significant challenges in trying to build on the example of Afrin. The returns file is but one example of how local sparks can ignite broader tensions in the north east. On 10 September, Sipan Hazni, a Kurdish former SDF soldier who had recently joined an integrated Syrian army unit, was kidnapped and brutally killed. Purported images of the murder circulated online, along with reports alleging that the killers were Arab tribesmen. As in August, protesters poured into the streets in Kurdish-majority towns and neighbourhoods, and some reportedly attempted to storm government facilities. This time, however, events escalated further in the town of Kobani (known in Arabic as Ayn al-Arab). The interior ministry deployed additional forces to the town, citing altercations that had left security personnel with injuries. Those forces arrested several demonstrators, then attempted to transport some of them from a prison in Kobani to Aleppo – in other words, from a facility still administered by former SDF-aligned personnel to one run by the central government. A prisoner reportedly lit a fire to protest the transfer, and nine detainees perished in the flames. Reactions in each camp underlined the challenges integration faces, but also its potential. Mistrust was evident, particularly in the episode’s early hours. An interior ministry official said some of those arrested were former SDF fighters, implying that elements of the former SDF that oppose integration were fanning unrest. Within SDF circles, the government’s deployment of reinforcements and attempt to transfer Kurdish detainees to facilities outside the north east bolstered concerns about further centralisation of security authority. Yet despite such misgivings, officials from both camps cooperated to quell the disturbance and signalled they would work together to investigate the incidents culminating in the prison fire. Mazloum Abdi’s role was particularly salient: meeting in Kobani with grieving family members and a range of local notables, he addressed concerns about the unrest and the integration process in his new capacity as adviser to President al-Sharaa. The combination of subsidy cuts and surging energy prices has hit the north east hard, with knock-on effects throughout the local economy. Meanwhile, economic conditions in the north east pose another political challenge, as the cost of living in areas previously governed by the SDF-linked administration has risen significantly. Though inflation is occurring throughout Syria, the surge in prices in the north east during recent months has been particularly acute. It has been driven, at least in part, by changes resulting from integration. When the former SDF-linked administration controlled the area’s oil extraction and economic policy, it provided cheap fuel and various subsidies to electricity generators, bakeries and other facilities, as well as to the vital agricultural sector. But as Damascus extended its writ, it scaled back these benefits, in keeping with its overall determination to maintain fiscal discipline. The combination of subsidy cuts and surging energy prices has hit the north east hard, with knock-on effects throughout the local economy. A steep hike in fuel prices announced by the government on 13 September exacerbated this dynamic, sparking protests in and beyond the north east. Insofar as north-eastern residents link the ensuing financial pain to integration, their faith in the process is fading. As fears resulting from the January military confrontation subside, Kurds in particular are liable to assess integration in terms of its practical impact. They have much to welcome: Kurds now enjoy legal recognition and state institutional roles that were hard to imagine under the previous regime, and the shift from SDF to state governance has eased some of their hardships, including difficulties with their educational diplomas, which previously were not recognised anywhere outside the north east. But, for now at least, the increased cost of living is undermining support among many who otherwise see integration’s benefits and sharpening grievances among those who oppose it. Eyes on the Prize The progress of integration to date is a testament to the foresight of the two sides’ respective leaders. But they need to remain focused on the significant challenges that lie ahead. The stakes are high and the payoff for further progress potentially great. Whereas any setback could have dangerous ramifications for the area’s stability, success could highlight constructive options for addressing governance and integration elsewhere – particularly in southern Syria, where the Druze-majority governorate of Suweida remains outside government control. While the local and geopolitical circumstances differ, the factors that will likely make or break integration in the north east would also be critical to an integration process in Suweida: incorporating local forces to lead in providing day-to-day security; ensuring that the area is well-represented in central government structures; and delivering clear economic gains and better services to the population. Having accomplished several of its priorities – notably extending the state’s institutions and command throughout the north east – Damascus ought to now focus on demonstrating the concrete benefits of integration. The more it is seen to improve security, governance and quality of life for Syrians in the north east, the more credibility integration will attain, including among those who remain understandably apprehensive of central state power after decades of suffering under the Assads. To that end, Damascus should clarify that the SDF’s former Asayesh personnel will form the long-term core of local security forces. It should also ensure that leaders such as Mazloum Abdi and Ilham Ahmad can play substantive, visible policymaking roles, including in drafting a new constitution – progress on which remains essential to Syria’s broader post-Assad transition. Mitigating economic pain in the north east will prove challenging in light of Syria’s fiscal constraints, but Damascus could discuss prospects for external aid to support integration with the U.S., as well as with European and Gulf Arab states. With the SDF now dissolved and several of its leading figures serving as senior government officials, integration may play out less as a negotiation between two parties and more as a mix of bargaining and collaboration among elements of the state. This shift arguably is already well under way locally, as illustrated by how the two camps have worked together to ease displaced persons’ return and to restore calm when tensions have boiled over. If Damascus aims to turn the north east’s integration into a model, building on that cooperation – including at the national level – would be an important way to strengthen its appeal. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. But the latest exchanges underscore a mutual willingness to use military escalation and economic disruption in gambits to strengthen positions at the negotiating table. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. While Israel has reduced the intensity of its attacks, it persists in conducting lethal strikes in the south, where it continues to occupy territory. Crisis Group expert David Wood says the continued Israeli assaults undermine the historic direct diplomacy that is happening between Israeli and Lebanese officials. Left unchecked, Israel’s attacks could sour relations between Tehran and Washington even further, making it even more difficult to reverse the escalatory cycle that has taken off in the Gulf. 10 July 2026 ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE UN Secretary-General António Guterres opened the Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva Monday by reiterating a call for a ban on what are called Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems, arguing that “some decisions must remain forever human – none more than taking a human life”. Crisis Group expert Issandr El Amrani says it is urgent to regulate the use of AI in warfare: AI-aided weapon systems are enabling rapid processing of targets with decreased human oversight, with potentially grave consequences for civilians, as seen during Israel’s war in Gaza and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. These “killer robots” need not be fully autonomous to render human oversight largely meaningless. More than 120 states, mostly from the Global South, have endorsed such a ban. But countries that have this technology, including the U.S., the UK and Russia, oppose it, contending that current provisions under international humanitarian law are sufficient. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Beijing characterised the missile test as part of routine annual training that comports with international law, stressing that it was not directed at another country. Australia, Japan and New Zealand raised objections, however, with Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong calling the test “destabilising” for the Asia Pacific and Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara describing it as “a grave concern” for the world. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the test sends a signal to the U.S. and allies that Beijing is determined to push back against what it views as attempts to contain China’s rise. The test took place on the same day that Australia signed a mutual defence agreement with Fiji. It will likely push other Asia Pacific countries both to deepen such cooperation and to accelerate their own military modernisation. SOUTH SUDAN On Sunday, opposition fighters killed James Kueth Makuach, commissioner of Akobo county in Jonglei state, in what President Salva Kiir’s government described as an “assassination”. Makuach had belonged to the party of former Vice President Riek Machar, who was arrested on sedition charges last year amid fighting between his loyalists and government forces. In April, Makuach defected to Kiir’s camp. The president then reappointed him as county commissioner, breaching South Sudan’s 2018 peace accord, which allotted this post to Machar’s group. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the Akobo attack, which also took the lives of two other government officials, is part of an escalation in clashes in Jonglei over the past week. But it appears to have been an act of political retribution rather than a push for territory or another military objective. Makuach’s killing underscores the dangers of proceeding with national elections planned for December with no political consensus in Juba and swathes of the country embroiled in civil strife. 3 July 2026 AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan flared again this week. On Sunday, Pakistani forces once again carried out strikes across the border in Afghanistan, saying they killed 29 militants. Islamabad said the strikes were retaliation for recent attacks inside Pakistan, including a Karachi assault that killed three security personnel. According to the UN, at least 28 civilians were killed and another 49 injured in the strikes. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban of sheltering anti-Pakistan militants, which Taliban officials deny. On Wednesday, Afghanistan said it carried out strikes inside Pakistan, targeting ISIS and other armed opposition groups. Islamabad denies Taliban accusations of harbouring such groups and noted that it had intercepted four drones launched from Afghan territory. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says outside mediators should push the sides toward practical border and security arrangements before the cycle of strikes and counterstrikes escalates further. NIGERIA Violence is again escalating in north-western Nigeria. Long plagued by bandits who engage in mass kidnappings for ransom, pillage and extortion, the region is also now seeing increased jihadist activity. Together, bandit and jihadist attacks killed over 150 people in Katsina, Kebbi, Sokoto and Zamfara states in June, a notable uptick from previous months. On 28 May, Islamic State Sahel Province claimed what appears to be its first reported attacks in the region, in which eighteen soldiers and one police officer were killed in Kebbi and Sokoto states. Amid this escalation, on 20 June prominent bandit leader Bello Turji claimed responsibility for deadly attacks on troops and declared his group ready for either peace talks or prolonged war with the government. If the bandit and jihadist threats are not reined in, says Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi, north-western Nigeria could become part of the wider belt of instability in the Sahel. SUDAN Fighting centred on El Obeid, North Kordofan’s state capital, has intensified in recent weeks as drone strikes increase and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) mobilise around the city, raising fears of encirclement and blockade. UN relief chief Tom Fletcher warned Tuesday that El Obeid risks becoming “another El Fasher”, referring to North Darfur’s capital, which endured a prolonged siege before falling to the RSF last October and suffering mass atrocities. Until the government addresses those weaknesses, the risk of more such violence will remain high – particularly in diverse areas where tensions built over fourteen years of war are still raw. 27 March 2026 IRAN With the Middle East war in its fourth week, the Trump administration submitted to Tehran, via Pakistani mediators, what U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff described as a “fifteen-point action list that forms the framework for a peace deal”. The plan, among other things, would reportedly require that the Islamic Republic give up its capacity to enrich uranium, which it has previously refused to do. Iran has countered with its own list of demands, including that the U.S. withdraw from all its military bases in the Gulf, which Washington has dismissed out of hand. Meanwhile, the U.S. is sending more ground troops to the region. A negotiated end to the conflict seems out of reach for now, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, as each side thinks its wartime position remains favourable. More likely is a protracted standoff or, worse, a dramatic escalation. IRAQ Fresh hostilities erupted this week between the U.S. and Iraqi militias backed by Tehran. These groups belong to an umbrella institution, the Hashd al-Shaabi, that is formally under the aegis of the Iraqi military commander-in-chief, though some of them operate independently. Those aligned with Iran have launched several rockets at U.S. bases in Iraq and neighbouring countries. A retaliatory U.S. airstrike on the Hashd headquarters in Baghdad killed fifteen fighters and another on a military facility in western Iraq claimed seven more lives. Meanwhile, the peshmerga in Iraqi Kurdistan, who are friendly to Washington, said Iranian missiles hit one of their bases in Erbil, killing six. The Iraqi government protested the infringements upon its sovereignty. But it lacks the leverage to stop the deadly exchanges, says Crisis Group expert Lahib Higel. The country is also facing an impending fiscal crisis, as oil sales have declined steeply with the Strait of Hormuz mostly shut. SUDAN UN agencies issued statements Tuesday protesting a “sharp increase” in drone warfare that is taking a mounting civilian toll. At least 70 people were killed the previous day when drones hit a hospital in East Darfur. Patients, doctors and nurses were among the dead. Another 28 civilians were killed in drone strikes in North Darfur and North Kordofan Thursday. Crisis Group expert Shewit Woldemichael says both main belligerents in Sudan’s war, the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), have stepped up their use of drones in an attempt to get an edge on the battlefield. Meanwhile, the risk of spillover into neighbouring countries is heightening, with the RSF taking a town on the Ethiopian border and fighting continuing on the Chadian frontier. 20 March 2026 CHAD - SUDAN A drone attack Wednesday killed seventeen people in Chad’s border town of Tine, including mourners gathered for a funeral and children playing nearby. The Chadian government accused the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan of launching the drone. In late February, the RSF had hit Chadian army positions in Tine, killing several Chadian soldiers. President Mahamat Déby ordered a total closure of the border with Sudan, which could have negative humanitarian consequences. The border has officially been closed since April 2023, but until now authorities have been allowing some refugees and aid shipments through. He also warned that Chad would retaliate for any further strikes on its territory, no matter who is responsible. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says Chad, which hosts around one million Sudanese refugees, increasingly risks getting drawn into the war in Sudan as fighting routinely spills across the border. IRAN Oil and gas prices soared and stock markets dived Thursday after Iran struck Qatar’s main natural gas facility, Ras Laffan. The Iranian attack came a day after Israel hit Iran’s South Pars gas field, one of the world’s largest. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these tit-for-tat attacks on hydrocarbon infrastructure signal a new phase in the conflict, now entering its fourth week, as a global energy crisis looms and Gulf Arab states are increasingly caught in the crossfire, with Saudi Arabia warning of military action against Iran as these states’ patience wears thin. NIGERIA Multiple suicide bombings Monday killed at least 26 people and injured over a hundred in Maiduguri, capital of Nigeria’s Borno state. The attacks mark the second deadliest incident in Maiduguri in the past five years. No group has yet claimed responsibility. The bombings come amid a surge of violence in the country’s north east, with both Boko Haram and the Islamic State-West Africa Province, an ISIS affiliate, launching lethal raids. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says the latest attacks indicate that these insurgencies may again be gaining momentum. The Nigerian government and its foreign partners should step up efforts to counter the new challenge and halt rising insecurity in other parts of the country. 13 March 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Drone strikes killed several people Tuesday night in Goma, capital of North Kivu province in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, including a French woman working with UNICEF and at least two other residents. The M23 rebels who hold the city blamed the Congolese government for the attacks. Kinshasa said an investigation is under way. Despite a formal ceasefire in their conflict, both the Congolese government and the M23 (backed by Rwandan troops) have been acquiring drones as a means of getting around enemy defences. Tuesday’s attacks, along with another in February that killed M23 spokesperson Willy Ngoma, mark a dramatic escalation in the conflict’s aerial warfare. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says Kinshasa, which has purchased Chinese and Turkish drones, is determined to use its new arsenal to show the rebels they are not safe in their bastions. But with civilian casualties mounting, the government’s growing reliance on drones could backfire by costing it international support. Having flexed its muscles, Kinshasa would be well advised to return to the diplomatic arena, pressing for Rwandan withdrawal from the country and returning to negotiations with the M23 with a stronger hand. IRAN Amid a widening Middle East conflict sparked by U.S.-Israeli strikes that began two weeks ago, the Islamic Republic effected only the second transition in its most senior post since the 1979 revolution that brought it to power. Mojtaba Khamenei has taken up the position of Supreme Leader, which his father Ali held from 1989 until his death on 28 February in the war’s opening salvo. The U.S.-Israeli campaign has continued unabated, doing significant damage. Iran has responded with drone and missile strikes in the Gulf and brought traffic in the Strait of Hormuz to a crawl. The first official statement attributed to the younger Khamenei was defiant in tone, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, highlighting the Iranian regime's desire to project continuity under duress, vis-à-vis both its foreign adversaries and its domestic opponents. But that ambition could be short-lived if Khamenei is targeted amid the hostilities or outmanoeuvred by other players in the regime's upper echelons. Many Iranians, meanwhile, are despairing at a leadership transition that so far promises more of the same. LEBANON Israel’s latest military escalation in Lebanon continued to wreak havoc this week. Since 2 March, when Hizbollah fired rockets toward Israeli territory for the first time in over a year, Israel has ramped up aerial bombardment, including of the capital Beirut, and forced hundreds of thousands to flee their homes. It has also sent more troops into southern Lebanon, with a view to establishing what it calls a “security zone” there. While Israel retains military superiority over Hizbollah, the Shiite party-cum-militia has put up a fight. On Wednesday, it launched a barrage of 100 rockets across the border, which triggered an especially brutal sequence of Israeli air raids. Crisis Group expert David Wood says neither of the belligerents appears ready to stop, even as Lebanese leaders scramble to find a diplomatic off-ramp. Already, the Lebanese public has paid a horrific price: the death toll has climbed to almost 700, and thousands more have seen their homes and communities destroyed. 6 March 2026 IRAN The U.S. and Israel launched massive airstrikes on Iran Saturday, hitting military installations and killing senior leaders, including Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. In retaliation, Iran fired missiles and drones at Israel, as well as U.S. bases and commercial infrastructure in Gulf states. The conflict's reverberations have quickly spread from the Indian Ocean to the eastern Mediterranean. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says Tehran looks prepared for a drawn-out confrontation, betting that it can steadily raise the psychological and economic costs to its adversaries, while maintaining cohesion at the top of the political system despite Khamenei’s demise. The U.S.-Israeli campaign appears open-ended, with no clear objective yet defined. Airstrikes can substantially degrade Iran's military capabilities but are unlikely to dislodge the regime, and even if they did, state collapse in Iran would risk unleashing far wider regional disorder. AFGHANISTAN - PAKISTAN Border clashes continued this week after Pakistan declared “open war” with Afghanistan last Friday. The declaration followed Taliban retaliatory cross-border attacks after Pakistani airstrikes on purported Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) targets in Afghanistan on 21 February. Pakistan then carried out another series of strikes on 27 February, including in Kabul. Islamabad accuses Taliban authorities of sheltering the TTP, which has stepped up attacks in Pakistan. Kabul denies it. According to the UN, the latest fighting has killed dozens of civilians in Afghanistan and displaced tens of thousands, with reports also indicating civilian casualties in Pakistan. Crisis Group expert Ibraheem Bahiss says a drawn-out conflict serves neither side's interests. Outside actors should press Islamabad and Kabul to de-escalate. ECUADOR The U.S. Southern Command said Tuesday Ecuadorian and U.S. forces had begun operations to curb organised crime in Ecuador. They first went after the Colombian armed group Comandos de la Frontera, which is active along the Colombian border. Ecuador’s military says the operations will continue indefinitely. While details are classified, news reports indicate that the U.S. played an advisory role, without putting troops on the ground. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says such cooperation is not new, but the latest announcement signals deeper U.S. involvement. Security ties have deepened as President Daniel Noboa aligns with the Trump administration’s preference for using military force to combat drug trafficking. 27 February 2026 CHAD - SUDAN Chadian authorities Monday announced the immediate closure of the country’s border with Sudan. The decision followed what N’Djamena described as “repeated incursions” linked to Sudan’s war, after clashes around the Sudanese border town of Tina involving the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces and militias aligned with Sudan’s army. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. PAKISTAN Police backed by soldiers reportedly killed more than 200 Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) fighters in raids throughout Balochistan, a south-western province next to Afghanistan, over the course of this week. The operations followed a rash of BLA attacks on police stations, military installations and residential areas that claimed 50 lives (33 civilians and 17 state personnel) over the weekend. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The leading opposition candidate, Robert Kyagulanyi of the National Unity Party (NUP), rejected the result, alleging widespread fraud. SYRIA Thousands demonstrated in the north east Tuesday against government forces’ expulsion of Kurdish fighters from Aleppo. In early January, the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) clashed with the Syrian army in Aleppo as negotiations to integrate Syria’s north east under central government control stalled. Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says Damascus cannot take the whole region militarily, but it will likely keep applying pressure on the SDF. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies.
